subtopic: IMMIGRANTS LANDING AT RIMOUSKI.
speechtext: 1 and 2. Rimouski is not a regular port of landing for immigrants. Occasionally steamship passengers destined to the Maritime Provinces desire for their own convenience to leave the vessel at Rimouski instead of continuing the journey to Quebec where the regular examination and debarkation takes place. Such persons are examined either by the agent at Rimouski or by Quebec officials who meet some of the vessels at Rimouski for the purpose of conducting the examination of passengers on the trip between that point and Quebec. No separate record is kept of persons leaving the vessel at Rimouski, and for statistical and other purposes they are reported as having landed at Quebec. Number and names asked for are therefore not available.

subsubtopic: LAURIER IN CONNECTION WITH THE JUSTICE LANDRY COMMISSION IN NEW BRUNSWICK.
speechtext:
A few days ago my hon, friend from the city of St. John (Mr. Pugsley) rose on a question of privilege, intending to deny certain statements made in this House, which he held to be unfounded in fact and deemed injurious to his honour a.s a citizen of Canada and a member of this House. My hon. friend did not only deny the words of which he complained, but he proceeded to read certain letters which bad been long dormant in the .archives of the provincial government at Fredericton, and which more than confirmed the denial he had made before the House. He was, however, stopped in this, on an obejction of the Prime Minister. It

*was held that on a question of privilege my 'hon. friend the member for St. John was particularly restricted to a denial, .and could not go beyond it.
You, Sir, ruled that the point was well taken and I have no fault to find with your ruling. Technically, I think it could not be impugned. You, Sir, held at the same time that the letters might be brought before the House in some other form or at some other time if my hon. friend from St. John deemed it advisable for his own sake to call attention to the matter.
The question has taken on a broader character than was at first indicated or than the simple question of privilege which was raised by my hon. friend. As I shall show the question involves not only the honour, the dignity and character of my hon. friend from St. John, but it involves also certain principles which apply to . the Government of the nation and which it is well to settle, if possible, here and now. The question to which I want to refer arose out of the discussion which took place in this House on the 6th June last, when my right hon. friend the Prime Minister informed the House that the hon. the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) had complained to him that the report made by Justice Galt, to which I need not refer now, was not an impartial report and that he had asked for a further investigation. He apprised the House that the Government had thought well to appoint another commission to review the report of Judge Galt which was to be composed of two members of the judiciary, the chief justice of New Brunswick, Sir Ezekiel McLeod, and a retired judge of the province of Quebec, Mr. Justice Tellier. I interjected in the debate that in my judgment, if this matter was to be reopened, the investigation should take place not through a Royal Commission composed of judges, or through a Royal Commission at all, but before a committee appointed by this House. In the course of the observations which I then made I referred to the attack which was made by the Minister of Public Works upon the character of Mr. Justice Galt. In reply to me the Prime Minister used these words:
My right hon. friend challenges the action we have taken and challenges the reflections which have heen made upon Mr. Justice Galt in the letter written to me from the Minister of Public Works. I should like to remind him that on a certain occasion one of his colleagues who sits beside him used infinitely stronger language, if my memory is correct, with regard to Mr. Justice Landry of the Supreme Court of New Brunswick, and he did so without any
reproof from my right hon. friend. I am perfectly willing to contrast the action which we have taken in this matter with that which my right hon. friend took on that occasion. Findings had been made by a commission of which Mr. Justice Landry was a member. Those findings reflected seriously upon a member of my right hon. friend's Government. The matter was brought to the attention of Parliament, and it was urged by a motion in this House that such finding should be disregarded.
The memory of the Prime Minister was altogether at fault when he stated that the report to which he referred of Mr. Justice Landry had been brought to the attention of the House and that my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) had urged that it be altogether disregarded. The report was brought to the attention of the House but it was brought not upon a motion to disregard it, but, on the contrary, it was brought upon a motion which was moved at the time by the hon. member for West Elgin, now the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers), to affirm the report and make it the basis of a motion of censure against my hon. friend from St. John who was at that time my colleague in the Government as Minister of Public Works. On the 5th May, 1909, the present Minister of Labour who was then, as now, the member for West Elgin, made a motion in this House but before doing so he recited that a commission had been appointed by the Government of New Brunswick to investigate the application of certain railway subsidies by the Government of New Brunswick at the time that my hon. friend the present member for St. John was a member of that Government, and he concluded:
The unanimous findings of the commission consisting of the Hon. Mr. Justice Landry and Messrs. F. MacDougall and A. I. Teed, appointed by the government of the province of New Brunswick by order in council dated June 5, 1908, and the authorized reports of the proceedings of the legislature of the said province during the session of 1908 set forth serious matters touching the public acts and conduct of Hon. Wm. Pugsley, formerly a member of the government of said province and now Minister of Public Works ;
That persons occupying high offices of state as constitutional advisers of His Excellency ought to be free from just reproach and from reasonable suspicion in respect of their public character and reputation;
That to this end the said findings in so far as they impugn acts or conduct of the said Hon. William Pugsley deserve the serious consideration of this House and demand such action thereupon as may be necessary to enforce worthy and proper standards of public duty.
I should observe here that in.proposing this motion of censure against a member of the then Government, the present hon. member for St. John, the hon. member for West

Elgin, relied altogether upon the proposition that a Royal Commission is a court of law and that the report of such a commission is the equivalent of a judgment. He refused altogether to consider the evidence upon which the report was founded and when challenged with the statement that the report was not in accordance with the evidence, he repeatedly stated that he did not care for the evidence, that he founded his accusation upon the report. Again and again he took the position that the report of a Royal Commission is equivalent to the judgment of a court of law.
It is important here and at all times, and perhaps more at this time than at any other, that we should exactly understand what is the effect of a Royal Commission, its purport and its object. We have only to refer to the statute, which is familiar to everybody in this House, to satisfy ourselves upon that point. The Government is required to institute a Royal Commission for the purpose of obtaining information, for the purpose of looking into some question of public concern, to find out the facts in connection with it and to report the. result to the Crown. A commissioner may simply hold an investigation and place the report before the Crown without expressing any opinion of his own, or he may, if he thinks fit, express an opinion of his own, as he generally does. But it was impossible to maintain for one minute, and no one would do so in this House under existing circumstances, that the report of a Royal Commission is equivalent to a judgment of a court of law. We have not only to look at the statute but at the practice. The Crown appoints a commissioner to investigate certain matters, the commissioner reports to the.Crown, and the Crown presents the report to Parliament, where it may become the subject of discussion by Parliament. It is a matter of elementary knowledge on the part of everybody that the decisions of a court of law are not to be reviewed by Parliament.
The judges are absolutely independent. Their decisions may be right or their decisions may be wrong, but they are the supreme arbiters appointed by the State to settle disputes between subject and subject, between man and man, and under no circumstances are they to be taken as amenable to Parliament; whereas, on the contrary, the reports of commissions are essentially to be reviewed by Parliament. The report of a commissioner, as is stated by all authorities on the matter, is

a useful form of information for the Government and for the public generally, but the opinion which is given by the commissioner is not binding. It is simply an opinion, respectable by the character of the man who expresses it, but it has no value except what value it can find from the truth and the correctness of the report which it places before the public. The present Minister of Labour and then the member for West Elgin (Mr. Crothers), when he made this motion, relied altogether on the report, refused to discuss the evidence, refused absolutely to go back of the report, and when it was objected to him that the report was not according to the evidence, he took the ground that it was of no concern to him that the judgment was equivalent to the judgment of a court. This is what he said on the occasion to which I refer, as reported at page 5655 of the Hansard of 1909:
Mr. Pugsley: I wish to correct the statement of my hon. friend, I was not the managing director of the company.
Mr. Crothers: I am simply making my observations bas^d upon the judgment of this court.
Mr. Pugsley: My hon. friend must pardon me. I say that there is nothing whatever in the evidence which would justify a statement of that kind, and the statement is absolutely untrue.
Mr. Crothers:	I am not here for the purpose of discussing the evidence in this ease.
Some hon. Members:	Oh, oh.
Mr. Crothers: Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to discuss the evidence in the case.
Mr. Pugsley: I am not surprised at that.
Mr. Crothers: I am here ' standing, on the judgment of a court.
Mr. Pugsley: If my hon. friend can And anything in the evidence which will justify some of the statements in the report, I shall be greatly obliged if he will refer to them.
Mr. Crothers: As I said a moment ago, I am not here for the purpose of discussing the evidence in this case. I am standing on the judgment of a court and while that judgment stands we have a right to assume that it is a righteous judgment.
I repeat that the case which was presented to the House in 1909 was certainly a very weak one when the hon. Minister of Labour in asking that censure be passed upon a member of the Government, upon a man who had been for more than 30 years in public life, a prominent citizen of Canada, basing this demand on certain alleged evidence, and making himself responsible for the charge, stated in so many words that he would have nothing to do with the evidence, would not look at it, said that he relied simply on the judgment. Well, I think, for my part, and I believe everybody will agree with me, that the case must have been

a very weak one, when any man, standing on the floor of this House to impugn the character of a fellow-member, will not at least refer to the evidence on which he bases his charge. It is quite true, as was said the other day by the Prime Minister, (Sir Robert Borden), that the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) on that occasion impugned the report of Mr. Justice Landry and his fellow Commissioners; he challenged it in many particulars and in so many words he showed discrepancies between the report presented by- the Commissioners and the evidence. Again and again the hon. member for St. John challenged the hon. member who made himself responsible for the charge to bring forward the evidence of the charge which he made, but upon every point he was met by *a refusal to produce the evidence. It now appears that there was a reason why the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Crothers), would not, on that occasion, go into the evidence, but relied upon the report. Let me repeat that the judgments of a Court are not to be reviewed by Parliament. It does not follow, and we cannot expect, that the judges never make mistakes. Judges are fallible like all other men. But'judges are generally selected from amongst a class of men trained in the law, trained to take evidence, and whose character gives a suggestion of security that their judgment will be impartial, the judgment of trained men, and will be generally correct. Although we are all prepared to admit that the judges oi the land generally give satisfaction, yet no one can pretend that they are infallible. They may make errors like everybody else; but if they make errors we must take them as they are, and Parliament has no right to pass upon them. But I repeat that no one will say that this Parliament can treat in the same the way the report of a commissioner, even if that commissioner be a judge. When he sits upon a commission he does not sit as a 'court of law; he is there simply as Mr. Justice So-and so, and his, opinions gain what value they may have from his character and what value there is in the report and the opinions which he expresses will be in accordance with the support which is given to them by the evidence. In this case, I repeat, my hon. friend the Minister of Labour, then a simple member of the House sitting for West Elgin, would not look at the evidence. I say that we can now understand why he would not go into the evidence. A report was made some time ago to the Legislature of New Brunswick, in reply to an address moved by a
member of that House in the following terms:
That a humble address he presented to His Honour the Lieutenant Governor, prayihg that he cause to be laid upon the Table of the House copies of all correspondence, between the Premier or any other member of the Provincial Government in the year 1908 and any person or persons relating to the appointment of Commissioners to investigate matters con. nected with the Central Railway Company and the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company; and also copies of any correspondence between the Premier or any other member of the Provincial Government and any person or persons relating to the report of such Commissioners.
.The report which was brought down by the Government in obedience to this order of the Legislature is composed of three letters which bear directly upon this subject. The first of the letters, not in order of the report, is dated May 21, 1908, and is addressed to the Hon. J. D. Hazen, K.C., M.P., Attorney General, Fredericton, by Mr. Fowler, then member for Kings and Albert, in this House, and now a senator.
House of Commons, Ottawa, May 21, 1908. My dear Hazen:
Yours to hand. I am sorry Trites has declined and I cannot understand why since I spoke to him and had his consent before I mentioned his name to you. There is a very good man, Fred C. Harris by name, who is manager of the Cape Tormentine Railway. There is also Capt. Geo. A. Coonan, of Harvey, A. Co., who built a portion of the Albert Southern Railway, and J. S. Armstrong, C. E., of Rothesay, so you can take your choice. X suggested to the surveyor-general that A. I. Teed, of St. Stephen, might be a good man if Mr. Thorne or W. S. Fisher would not act.
I presume this Tefers to acting in the capacity of commissioner for the investigation.
I still think that you should have a junior counsel to assist Powell in this matter and the small additional expense should not stand in the way as this is a very important thing for us. I believe we can put the genial "Wm. out of business if this matter is properly handled"
There was the animus-"we can put the genial Wm. out of business." The letter proceeds:
Mr. Borden was much pleased to hear that the boys in New Brunswick were so strongly with us on the Aylesworth Bill.
Sincerely yours,
George W. Fowler.
Then there is another letter from Mr. H. A. Powell, who was employed as counsel in the case, which went to show that, as suggested in the letter, if the matter were properly handled, they could put "the

genial William out of business." The letter reads:
Powell and Harrison, barristers, solicitors, j	notaries, etc.,
Hon. J. D. Hazen, Attorney-General, Fredericton, N.B.
St. John, N.B., March 31, 1909.
Dear Hazen:-As I 'phoned you last evening, the report of the commissioners was sent forward by express. The Act authorizing the investigation directed the report to be addressed to the Provincial Secretary to be by him laid before the Governor. This language we interpreted literally and the report is directed to the Provincial Secretary and he can lay it before the Governor, which I presume will be done at once. After that I suppose it will be laid on the table of the House. The Times has printed a number of copies, I do not know how many, which they will forward to you in a day or two.
You will notice in the report there are some corrections made in writing and the errata are gathered into a fly leaf and will be bound with the report. I regret very much that this errata had to be made. Mr. McDougall was very strongly of the opinion that I should have as little as possible to do with the final making up of the rsport, inasmuch as the charge might be made that I and not the Commissioners got up the report. I spent all day Monday with them in Moncton. At that time the report had not been completely drafted and a good deal of the proof had not been read. It was arranged between us that Mr. McDougall would send me down the proof and I would revise it and make all necessary corrections. On Saturday Judge Landry rang me up and arranged that I would go Aip on Monday morning to finally revise their work. On Sunday, however, Mr. McDougall rang me up and told me that he and Judge Landry had finally revised it themselves and the report was all printed, and consequently not to come uo.
On Monday morning Judge Landry rang me up again wanting to know why I had not gone up. Monday night the Commissioners all gathered at St. John with the report completely printed. There are a few things that I would like very much to have had different from what they are. In the first place, I urged on them the great undesirability, in view of you pushing your claim against the Dominion Government for increased subsidy, of minifying the cost of the fifteen mile section and branches as is done on pages fifty-six and fifty-seven of the report, and I drew up myself a statement which could not be used against your contention, but the Commissioners determined to insert the statements on pages fifty-four, fifty-five and fifty-six.
The reference to the Intercolonial on page fifty-five struck me as affording scope to Pug-sley and the newspapers to attack the Commissioners on the absurdity of the comparison between the fifteen mile section and the Intercolonial so I had them insert the words "As was intimated." They had an error of fact in respect to the bridges on the fifteen mile section which I had them correct. Another error was the reference to the provincial engineer having made the estimate; it was the company's engineer.
Another matter which I am sorry has gone in as it did inasmuch as it will give the OpfSir Wilfrid Laurier.]
position press an opportunity to make an attack on the commissioners is the statement at the bottom of page 18 and top of page 19 to the effect that it appears conclusively from the evidence that the whole $250,000 par value of the 3 per cent bonds had been guaranteed and delivered to the company up to August 6, 1903. The only evidence to that effect was an impression Mr. Shadbolt had that the whole $250,000 of 3 per cent bonds which were delivered to him at that time had the provincial guarantee on them. Mr. Shadbolt may have been right in his impression, but the statement is not consistent with the Order in Council with reference to guaranteeing the bonds. In the following two paragraphs the reference to the guaranteeing of the whole $450,000 bonds is somewhat misty. The criticism in this connection should be directed solely to the $250,000 of bonds which were guaranteed for the construction of the fifteen-mile section.
I drafted the portion of the report referring to the guaranteeing of the bonds, but Judge Landry himself changed it in the respects I have mentioned. Fortunately-
And this is why I understand the hon. gentleman from West Elgin (Mr. Crothers) was so chary about touching the evidence:
Fortunately the fellows on the other side will know nothing about the matter, and if the statement is challenged the reporter has Mr. Shadbolt's evidence much stronger than he gave it. Furthermore, I think the judge is right in the statement he makes and it is literally true although the whole $250,000 of the bonds had not then been made use of by the company. Since there is evidence to support the finding I suppose their finding will be accepted.
I suppose both you and Mr. Fleming will go into the matter of the report quite thoroughly when the discussion of it comes up in the House. If there is any matter that you want light thrown upon, or if you want to know the particular source of any information used in the statements, let me know and I will give it to you. It might be a good thing for me to run through the report and mark in the margin the sources of information. Although I would like to have seen several things put more forcibly than they have been and the responsibility for the misappropriation shown	to rest more on Pugsley's
shoulders, I think you will find that the report is pretty strong.
Yours very truly.
(Signed) H. A. Powell.
Then there is another letter from my hon. friend, the then member for North Toronto, now Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), which reads- as follows:
House of Commons, Ottawa, April 14, 1909.
Dear Mr. Hazen :-
I telegraphed you this morning re the Comm. Reports and trust you have sent me a number. As to copy of evidence I put that in in case you have it printed wbflch probably you have not. It is, I suppose, voluminous.

Why I did so was for this reason. Pugsley so far as now appears will try to bluff the matter out of the House here as not pertaining to Federal affairs. He will say that the report is not based on evidence and that he will, after getting a copy of the evidence, issue a statement showing this to be so. That will be his defence. We propose to get after him here before he gets a copy of the evidence, hut if by any possibility he does get it then we need the evidence to meet him here.
I presume the evidence will not be available in printed form for some time. If he gets a copy I hope you will see that several copies are made at the same time and that we get one or two here.
I have not seen full report hut what I have seen is pretty straight goods.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) G. E. Foster.
Now, Sir,- this is the case to which my hon. friend, the member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) wants to call the attention of the House. In 1909 it was sought to censure an hon. member-and a motion was made to that effect-upon a report which is in contradiction in many points of the evidence; upon a report taken by itself independent of the evidence. I lay this as the foundation. I am sure nobody will contradict the statement that any report of -a commission without the evidence is simply the opinion of a man, and has no foundation whatever upon which can be based any ground at all for a motion of censure. Nobody in this House, I am sure, will contend that an -hon. member is liable to censure upon the report of a commission, no matter who the commissioner is, unless evidence accompanies the report to justify it. It would be monstrous; it would be unfair; it would be unjust, to condemn a man simply upon the opinion of a fellow-man without the production of evidence to substantiate that opinion. 'The opinion may be -right or it -may -be wrong, but whether it is right or wrong, the Parliament of Canada, when it is asked to pronounce upon a matter of this kind, has the right to have the evidence before it so that every *member may come to a conclusion whether -the report is or is not justified. The correspondence which I -have read to you, Sir, has proved conclusively that this matter was placed before the House before the evidence was brought out, so that there should be -an ex parte verdict upon the opinion of the commission, not upon the evidence itself. Luckily, the truth -has come out at last, and the member for St. John city, upon the evidence that has now been presented, is fully vindicated out of the mouth of his own adversaries.

subtopic: ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF THE NAVAL SERVICE.
speechtext: It has been my custom, Mr. Chairman, when taking up the estimates of the Naval Department that relate particularly to naval affairs, to make a statement covering the operations of the department during the twelve months ended March 31 of the last fiscal year. It is desirable, I think, that I should follow that custom on the present occasion.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
During the last session I gave a summary of the operations of the Naval Service Department from the commencement of the war. That -statement will be found on page 3002 of Hansard for the session of 1916. While it is unnecessary again to submit the information already given in that report, I desire to bring it up to the end of the fiscal year 1916-17.
Headquarters.
During the last year the work of the department continued to increase and expand. Some idea of the increase in the amount of work at headquarters may be had from the following statements:
Letters and telegrams received:
January, 1916	 5,079
March, 1917	 8,464
Increase	 3,389

speechtext:
Why did the minister
not give the figures for the same months in each year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
I gave the figures for the last month before the end of the fiscal year ended March 31, 1917, to show the tremendous increase that has taken place since, my last statement was made.
On August 1, 1914, the total personnel of the headquarters staff amounted to 127 persons. On March 31, 1917, the total personnel amounted to 256 persons.

The personnel employed in radiotelegraphy in the Dominion is 404, of whom 137 are in the Government employ.
Of the 43 coast stations 42 are owned by the Government. Those located on the west coast and Hudson bay are operated directly by the Department of the Naval Service. Those situated on the Great Lakes and east coast with certain exceptions, are operated by the. Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company, Limited, under contract. Since the outbreak of the war certain stations on the east coast have been taken over and operated directly by the department exclusively for naval purposes.
As regards construction, the department has maintained the different stations under its charge in an efficient and up-to-date condition, so that the Canadian service compares favourably with that maintained elsewhere.
The enforcement of the Radiotelegraph Act has been carried out by the responsible officers of the department in an efficient manner. That section of the Act calling for compulsory equipment of wireless apparatus on certain steamers has been well observed by the shipowners, and no attempts to evade the requirements of the law have been reported.
During the year 141 radiotelegraph operators were examined for certificates of proficiency in radiotelegraphy, of whom 87 were successful. To date there have been 176 certificates of proficiency issued by the department.
The regular work of the stations has been carried out so far as permissible under war conditions, and a surprising increase in both the number of messages handled and revenue collected is shown. The west coast stations operated directly by the department handled 1,741,420 words, as against 1,103,395 last year, and the total revenue accruing was $18,201, as against $7,394.50 last year, an increase of 146 per cent; this is the largest revenue credited to the west coast in the history of the service.
In conclusion, I may say that the operation of the radiotelegraph service has, during the past year, continued to prove the wisdom of the Government's policy of government ownership and control, and the expenditures made on its account are being fully justified.
Stores Branch.
During the year ending March 31, 1917, the activities of the Stores Branch have

been maintained and extended as the requirements of the service demanded.
As in the past, the requirements of the following services have been filled in addition to the Naval Service proper (Imperial and Canadian), viz-Hydrographic Surveys, Tidal and Current Surveys, Radiotelegraph Service, Fishery Protection Service, Life Saving Service, Fishery Patrol Service, Fish Breeding Service, and other fishery services.
Notwithstanding that considerable difficulty has been experienced in obtaining supplies, *mere especially me'tals and textiles, the requisite reserves have been maintained at both dockyards, and in certain instances, very materially increased. A further agreement with the Admiralty to supply Imperial ships in the Pacific with clothing and victualling stores has necessitated a considerable addition to the stock previously carried. The recruiting of the Royal Naval Canadian Volunteer Reserve for service overseas in the Royal Navy and for the Canadian Patrol Service has also necessitated the maintenance of further reserves of clothing supplies.

Considerable purchases have been made on account of the Imperial Government, and, in a lesser degree, on behalf of allied governments.
Contracts have been made for the charter of thirteen vessels of varying dimensions. The charter of ten others expired during the year, and were not renewed. The total expenditure involved was $294,266.85.
The facilities for issuing supplies of all descriptions to the various services have been fully maintained. The total issues made from Halifax dockyard were $592,926, and from Esquimalt dockyard, $411,270. In addition to the service rendered to ships and establishments of this department and other Canadian Government departments, material assistance has been afforded to Imperial ships calling at Canadian dockyards. Issues to Imperial ships from Halifax dockyard amounted to $254,309, and .from Esquimalt dockyard to $183,624. In a lesser degree, similar assistance has been afforded to ships of allied governments.
The Imperial .authorities continue to avail themselves of our facilities at both dockyards to keep large reserves of special .stores for His Majesty's ships in the Atlantic and Pacific. These are accounted for and in every way cared for in the same manner as Canadian istores. Particular care has to be given to ordnance stores and ammunition, for which special facilities are provided.
The value of the stores in stock at the beginning Of the year was $409,618 at Halifax, and $351,611. at Esquimalt. The value of the stores in stock at the end of the yeak was $628,006 at Halifax, and $477,989 at Esquimalt.
Supplies of coal have been well maintained on both coasts for Imperial and Canadian ships. The total receipts at Halifax amounted to 78,575 tons, and at Esquimalt to 31,711 tons. The issues at Halifax were 77,733 tons, and at Esquimalt 29,626 tons. In addition, .the following were handled on direct charge to the ships : At Halifax, 138,509 tons, and at Esquimalt, 16,545 tons. The following fuel oil was purchased at Esquimalt and Halifax: 107,000 gallons.
Transportation.
During 1916-17 the work in connection with transportation has greatly increased. The director of overseas transport has general control of the traffic inland, by rail
or otherwise, its reception and storage at points of shipment, the allocation of the Cargoes to the different ships, and the storage on board. The Department of the Naval Service is responsible for the movements of these ships, the supply of sufficient tonnage to meet transportation' demands, and the routing of same, .as well as the responsibility of keeping the Admiralty informed on all questions of transport.
Through co-operation between the director of overseas transport and the Naval Service Department, the transportation problems have been, to a large extent, overcome, .and .a high degree of efficiency has been maintained. All expenses in connection with this service .are defrayed by the department on behalf of the Imperial Government, on .presentation of duly certified invoices.
Contracts have been made for the supply of bunker coal as necessary. Two hundred and thirty thousand tons have been purchased from Canadian firms for transports during the .past year. Arrangements have also been made as necessary for repairing, and fitting ships for special purposes, and for the supply of such provisions, stores, .and gear as are required while the ships are in Canadian ports.
The average export movement for the year ended 31st March, 1917, amounted to more than 200,000 tons per month, or roughly, eight fully loaded freight trains of material per day. The monthly total now exceeds 360,000 tons, and the sailings average two per diem. The Overseas Transport Organization has worked with the greatest regularity and despatch. Practically no delays have been experienced throughout the period of the review. The movement has been rendered possible only by the ready co-operation of all transportation companies with the staff of the .service, in all matters. During the financial year of 191617, a total of 386 sailings, comprising 2,429,829 tons cleared from Canadian ports. These figures show a large increase over 1915-16 in which year 198 sailings comprising 970,911 tons cleared, an increase amounting to 206 sailings, comprising 1,458,918 tons. The thanks of the department are due to the Canadian Pacific Railway company, for the service of a number of experienced

transportation officers, as well as for their ready co-operation at all times. To the efforts of the director of Overseas transport and his staff are largely due t'he success of the whole service. To the success of this service is undoubtedly due the increasing magnitude of the orders now being placed for the products of the mines, forests, fields, and factories o-f Canada by the Imperial and allied governments.
Fisheries Protection Service.
The vessels of the Protection Service have, during the past year, carried out the duties of guarding the fishing grounds along the east and west coasts and in the Great Lakes, -and enforcing the fishery laws. Particularly valuable work was done by these vessels in watching the United States fishing vessels operating outside the three mile limit.
The Fisheries Protection Service vessels were also utilized under the Naval Service in connection with mine-sweeping and patrol duties.
Life Saving Service.
The Life Saving stations were kept in an efficient condition throughout the season of navigation. Owing to the increased use of motor-boats by the fishermen along the coasts the demands upon the Life Saving stations for assistance have been gradually reduced, in many instances one boat -being able to render assistance to another without aid from the Life S-aving crew.
Tidal and Current Survey.-This survey has been successfully carried on in new areas along the coasts and rivers of Canada. A large portion of the navigable waters have now been covered by the survey and navigation has been greatly facilitated as a result thereof. The information obtained is published annually in Tide Tables and pamphlets.
Hydrographic Survey.-Work has been carried out on the east coast at Halifax harbour and at the mouth of the St. Lawrence; in the Great Lakes along the shores of Lake Superior and in Kingston harbour on the west coast, in the vicinity of Queen Charlotte Islands and in the different navigable passes. A number of new charts of the areas surveyed have been prepared and will be published shortly. The activities of this branch of the service have during the past three years, been greatly reduced owing to the enlistment of a number of the permanent staff for active service overseas.
Accountant's Branch.-The total expenditure of the Naval Service Department dur-
TMr. Hazen.l
ing the fiscal year 1916-17 was $16,416,839.36. Out of this amount $4,242,489.99 were expended from the regular appropriation and $4,761,991.96 out of the war appropriation; $7,412,357.41 were expended on account of the Imperial Government, which amount is recoverable.
That in brief measure, is an account of the activities during the year of the Department of Naval Service. There are a great many details which would be interesting but which it would not be proper to make public at the present time. The work of the department, due in very large measure, I feel satisfied, to the active efforts and energies of the deputy -minister, the Director of Naval Service and the other heads of departments, has proceeded most satisfactorily. This work has very greatly increased as was shown -by the increase which has occurred among the clerks of the lower classes employed in the department. The work will likely increase during the coming year if the war continues. Our work in connection with dockyards and the ships of the Allies coming and going has been of the most satisfactory character. There has been little or no trouble in- dealing with them and little or no irritation has been caused in any respect. The different items will come before the committee, and I will be very g}ad to furnish such information as I can to hon. members.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: The -minister only mentioned one ship, the Niobe. What has become of the other?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
The Rainbow is still in
British Columbia.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
What about
the Niobe? I have seen a report that the Government contemplated breaking up the Niobe and sending her to the scrap heap.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I saw something of that kind in the newspapers, but I do not always believe what I see there. I would have been shocked if that had been the intention of the Government, although I have seen worse things done by this Government. Where is the Niobe?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
We are making the only
use of the Niobe that is possible. It was not possible to use the Niobe for active service. We are using her as a depot ship in Halifax harbour. Nav-al people are constantly coming and going from the West Indies and other places, and we use the

Niobe for what you might call a naval barracks. She is also used as a training ship. But it is impossible to use her for any defensive purpose at the present time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: The Niobe was purchased for the purpose of being used as a training ship.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: At the outbreak of the war and for a short time afterward we used the Niobe for certain patrol purposes on the Atlantic coast. The patrol has been carried on by the ships of His Majesty's navy and the Niobe has for some time not been in a position for service in that respect.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: The Rainbow, I understand, is being used for the protection of the nsheries on the Pacific?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: It has been used all along on the Pacific.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: How many sailors have you on board?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: The Rainbow carries about 270 men.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Are they all Canadians?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I do not think so. I would think that a good many would be Britishers. A great many are men who have been in His Majesty's navy.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
How many
boats have we engaged in the protection of the fisheries on the Pacific ocean?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: We have three fishery protection vessels on the Pacific coast. Two, of the type that is employed in the protection of the Irish fisheries, were built at Dublin four or five years ago. The other is an older boat and has been in the service a longer time. In addition to that we charter another vessel called the Lillooet.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: What about the Naval College? How many students are there?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
The college has had its best year in its history. At present I think there are between 30 and 40 students, practically all we can now accommodate. These come from all parts of the country. There is one from Dawson City, but most of them are from the interior, from Ontario, and a number from Montreal and other points in Quebec. The college is doing well, making good progress, and were it not that the Minister of Finance is urging us to keep down our expenses, I would have asked for a considerable appropriation for the erection of a more suitable building. The old 264
hospital in the Naval Yard, which is now used as the main college building, has become inadequate for the purpose. A new building must be provided, and when that is done, if we continue to have a Naval College, as I hope we shall, the building should be entirely adequate. Those who have gone through the college and entered the Navy have had splendid records. Even if a student does not enter the Navy, the training and education which he receives at the Naval College are of great value to him in civil life, just as the course at the Royal Military College equips a young man for other callings than military life. I am satisfied that, from the development of the last few years, especially the last two years, the college will become one of the most important public institutions in Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: What is the nature of the education? Does the student, in addition to instruction in astronomy, geography, mathematics, etc., receive any practical naval instruction?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Of-course, all of the instruction looks towards service in the Navy. During their course at the college the young man receives minor practice on small ships. If he decided to enter the Navy, he spends two 'and a half years on one of His Majesty's ships.	.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: How many years is the college course?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Three years.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: What success has attended the recruiting for the British Navy under Sir Rupert Guinness.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
It is almost la mistake to say that the recruiting was under him. He came here with a letter .addressed to me by Mr. Balfour, who was then First Lord of the Admiralty, .and he h.ad authorization from the Admiralty, with our approval to enlist men from Canada for the navy. But his authorization was to enlist them at the rate of pay of the Royal Navy, Which is, I think, 36 cents a day. It would have been impossible to enlist men in Canada on those terms. That was explained to him. We communicated with the Admiralty and told them that we were willing to receive and enlist men for the navy, paying them the same rate as is paid in the Canadian navy, which is practically the same as the rate of pay to the troops for overseas service, and that we were willing to .place those men .at their disposal. We feared that



this might not be acceptable ito the Admiralty owing to the objection to having men on the 'some ship under such different nates of pay, but, on consideration, the Admiralty saw no objection. So we arranged to recruit the men with the 'assistance of Sir Rupert Guinness. We organized recruiting boards and great service was rendered by some gentlemen, for instance Mr. jEmelius Jarvis, of Toronto. We turned the Montreal commissioner's office into a recruiting office under the direction of Mr. Ross and the officials of the department, including the assistant secretary, Mr. Fennell, who were most active. In this way we succeeded in enlisting 1,600 men. We found that a great many men who would have preferred service in the navy if the Admiralty had asked us for recruits early in the war, at the time when we suggested such recruiting to them, hut when the British Government said that they pref erred that we should confine our attention to recruiting for the land forces, had akeady enlisted in the army and had gone overseas. But we enlisted 1,600 men, who were sent overseas, and who, I have no doubt, have been of very considerable help. Sir Rupert Guinness 'and his wife, who is a talented speaker, were of great assistance. They addressed recruiting meetings and Canadian Clubs in different parts of the country.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: The minister has given us a sketch of the work of his department. I presume that most of that work will be paid for out of the War appropriation.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I said we had spent about $17,000,000. About $4,000,000 in all was paid out of our appropriation for the ordinary work of the department.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: For the year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Yes. Another $4,000,000 to be charged up to the War Measures Act and to the War Appropriation, and the balance of the money spent for supplies and purposes of the Imperial navy, and of certain of the Allied navy, because at times Italian and French ships come to our ports, and we have to furnish supplies. That money all comes back to us, but the moneys we have spent ourselves would amount to $9,000,000, of which one-half would be payable out of the appropriation made by Parliament. The other half would come under the War Measures Act.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Would the minister be at liberty to tell us what progress Mr. Nor-
[Mr Hazen.]
cross is making in connection with his shipbuilding for the British Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: We have been following that work with a very great deal of care. Mr. Norcross, I am glad to say, volunteered his services and rendered us very valuable assistance. We had not enough officials in the department to undertake it, and we had to accept the services of volunteers. This work is progressing satisfactorily, but not so rapidly as we hoped. There is difficulty about getting boilers and engines, which has caused delay. However, a number of vessels have been launched, and we hope to have a number of them in patrol service in such places as the British Government desires to place them. The British Government asked our department to undertake that work, and we are doing it, greatly assisted by Mr. Norcross and certain other gentlemen. The work is being performed in certain places in Canada. In Quebec the work is being done by George Davies, in Montreal by the Canadian Vickers, in Toronto by Norcross and Poison. At Collingwood and Port Arthur, and dif-' ferent points in Canada, work is being done. On the whole, I think it is going ahead satisfactorily, but there are delays in obtaining material, and it has not proceeded as quickly as we hoped it would at the time the orders were placed.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
We have sent over a number of young men who are active in the .motor-boat patrol service. From along the St. Lawrence several young men have gone, and my information is that they are in the motor-boat patrol, although some of them did not go over for that purpose. It is interesting to know that the education they received as a matter of pleasure on the rivers and waters of Canada has proved of such great benefit to them and to the Empire at the present time. Has the minister any information he can give us about the number of young men who are in that service and what they are doing?
M3r. HAZEN:	Nearly 300 young men
entered as sub-lieutenants, and over a hundred young men for duty as chief motor mechanics and motor mechanics in this branch of the Imperial service. It is known as the Auxiliary Motor Boat Patrol System. We have practically sent over about four hundred young men for that purpose.
Naval service-To provide for the maintenance and upkeep of ships, naval college, dockyards at Halifax and Esquimalt and Royal Naval Canadian Volunteer Reserve, $1,000,000.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
What vessels does the
minister consider naval vessels? -

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: All vessels practically engaged in naval service. For instance all vessels that are engaged in the patrol service all around our coast, watching to see that no naval base is established, and on the lookout for any submarine that might appear.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: How many of them are there?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Something like thirteen or fifteen, I think.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Of the larger types?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
I will get the list.
Mr. KY'TE: But there is a larger number of motor boats employed, is there not?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Yes, but they are hardly regarded as naval vessels. There are a number at Sydney and Halifax used in connection with the vessels at those ports.
Mr. MARCH,: Has anything been seen of the enemy in Canadian waters since the war broke out?

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
It is pretty hard to answer. In the early days of the war there was scarcely a day we did not receive a report of submarines being seen. All shipping was stopped on the St. Lawrence. No ships were allowed to go out of Quebec.
This, was done because the statement came from lighthouse keepers that several submarines had been seen in the lower part of the Gulf. We used to hear reports, too, of submarines being seen around the Island of Cape Breton; the member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) no doubt remembers the report that was sent in about their having been seen in the Bras d'Or lakes. They were reported also as being off the coast of Maine. At one time the reports were backed by such evidence that the Naval Department of the United States sent ships down there and were in communication with us in regard to the matter. In nearly all these cases, however, investigation proved that the reports were unfounded. My own belief is that enemy submarines have not been near our coast. We have received even this year reports of that kind that seemed to be well verified, but on investigation we came to the conclusion that it could not have been submarines that were seen.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
New York harbour was
closed for part of one day.
264J	,	,

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Yes. We have thought
that there would be more possibility of enemy ships operating further to the south if they were on this side of the Atlantic at all. Of course, the submarines can do much more effective work by remaining neaT the other side, near their bases, in the path of vessels crossing to the British Isles. Most probably it would only be for spectacular purposes that they would make a trip over to this side. We are taking every step that we can take in order to combat this danger. I do not think it is possible, having regard to the means of protection that arp being adopted, for a submarine base to be established anywhere along the coasts of Newfoundland or the Maritime Provinces, or in the Straits of Belle Isle. At one time there was a general theory that a submarine base might be established along the Straits of Belle Isle, and that district was quite carefully watched. Up to the present, however, we have had no evidence to lead to the conclusion that any submarine base has ever been established on this 6ide of the Atlantic in Canadian territory.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: There has been no difficulty between the British Admiralty and this country since the war began in respect of naval matters?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: No, the arrangements have been very satisfactory. Everything in connection with dockyards, stores and all such matters has gone very smoothly indeed.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: My hon. friend, who has spoken so favourably about the Royal Canadian Navy, will, I assume, do nothing to repeal the Naval Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman must not ask me to pledge myself; it is very dangerous to make a promise in these times.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: At all times.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that everything is smooth as between the Canadian Naval Department and the British Admiralty. We are building ships for the British Government; we are employing many men; the patrol of our sea coast is under the direction of the Canadian Naval Department. My hon. friend has excellent officers; he has naval cadets; his naval college is working in perfect order. Besides, my hon. friend has been able to recruit for the British Admiralty during the

year. On the whole, in this respect, my hon. friend is possibly the least objectionable of all the ministers. We are very fortunate indeed in having our Royal Canadian Navy, not only for election time, but for all times.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: The member for Rouville (Mr, Lemieux) might have added that, as a fortunate and happy conclusion of the antinaval. campaign, the present Government has elevated to the Senate Mr. L'Esperance, the late member for Montmagny, who had given notice in the House of a resolution to repeal .the. law creating the Canadian Navy. He was impelled, however, to withdraw the notice of this resolution. Subsequently he was made Chairman of the Quebec Harbour Board, and, as a faithful reward for his services, he has been raised to the Senate and has voted for conscription. This gentleman was roundly denounced in 1911.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I am not surprised that there is no increase in. this vote. I would imagine that the protection of the fisheries is almost a sinecure now. There is no poaching in Canadian waters.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Oh, yes; we have to watch Pur waters all the time. Only the other day an American vessel was seized within the ithree mile limit on the Nova Scotia coast. A few weeks before that, another one had been seized. A large fishing fleet is off the Nova Scotia coast now, and we have to *watch the vessels as a cat watches a mouse to prevent their coming within the three mile limit. We have not, however, spent the money voted last year. We .are asking for the same amount this year as last. Last year the gross amount spent was $299,000. A portion of the gross expenditure was transferred to the War Appropriation vote, which left the net expenditure at $145,000. I doubt if we shall spend more than half of the amount we .are asking for this year.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Why was part transferred to the War Appropriation vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Because after these boats had finished with the patrol service they were used in connection with the Naval Service.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: On the Atlantic coast?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I quite realize that we must keep a watch in our territorial waters, because if our cruisers were not there the American fishing vessels might indulge in poaching. I am happy to believe-indeed, I have reason ' to believe that relations .between Canada and the United States .are very much more friendly to-day than some years ago, when we had very serious trouble over the fisheries question. In view of this, I think the expenditure on the fisheries protection service, especially on the Pacific coast, might be very much reduced. Pelagic sealing has been abolished, and I should think that we have not much to fear from American poachers in our northern Pacific waters, although farther .south, in .the vicinity of the San Juan straits, a closer watch no doubt has to be kept. Perhaps my hon. friend will tell us just what the conditions are.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
I do not think the fisheries protection fleet ever had anything to do with the protection of the sealing. As my right hon. friend says, pelagic sealing is now a thing of the past, and there is no expenditure necessary for that purpose. In a very short time we expect to receive .a very considerable sum of money under the terms of the treaty that was made. We received $200,000 dn advance, when the killing of seals was prohibited for a period of five years, contrary to the opinion of out scientific men, who- thought that step undesirable. In a very short time we shall be getting 15 per cent of the hides from America, 10 per cent from Japan, and 15 .per cent from Russia.
Although excellent relations exist between Canada and the United States at the present time, that does not prevent individual American fishermen from coming within the three-mile limit and taking our fish if they think they can get away in safety. It is just as necessary to keep a close watch to-day as when onr relations were not so good as at present. The right hon. gentleman referred to the 5 p.m. protection service on the Pacific.
We have to keep a watch upon

the northern Pacific waters where there is a great deal of poaching by American fishing vessels. A large American fleet goes up to the North every year for the purpose of catching halibut, which are caught nearly altogether outside of territorial waters.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
What is the
base of that fleet?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Ketchican, in Alaska. Farther south, near the international boundary, a watch has also to be kept. I would again point out that the fact of our good relations with the United States at the present time does pot to any extent reduce the expense of our fisheries protection service, because there is just the same temptation now as formerly for an American citizen to get the best fishing he can wherever he can get it, and if he is allowed to come within the three-mile limit, he will do so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Would the minister say what action was taken in regard to the proposed regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
My hon. friend refers to the treaty that was entered into. The treaty provided that each country should appoint a commissioner, and that the commissioners should prepare regulations for the control of the fisheries in waters contiguous to the international boundary. The Congress of the United States never passed the legislation that was necessary to make that treaty effective, and that the Government of which my hon. friend was a member appointed Professor Prince, and that the United States Government appointed Prof. Starr Jordan. Those gentlemen made the regulations, and they were published. The Parliament of Canada at once, under the terms of the treaty, passed the necessary legislation in good faith to make them effective, 'but the United States Congress refused to pass such legislation on their part. I had a talk with the present President, Mr. Wilson, about it, and came to the conclusion that nothing could be done. Special interests in the United States
prevented Congress from doing what they undertook to do under the treaty,

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.

Fishing was not good in
the early part of the season. It is improving, and on the whole I think it is better than it was last year. speechtext: Might I ask if the list the minister handed me contains the names of all motor boats employed by the Government in Nova Scotia waters?

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
