subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Some little time ago, I referred to a scheme which was favourably considered by the minister in connection with the sardine fisheries in the counties adjacent to Charlotte. The idea was to give to Canadian buyers of sardines a preference over other buyers. My hon. friend stated that the object was to encourage the establishment of canning interests in Charlotte county promoted by the late Sir William Van Horne. After the decision had been arrived at to impose a condition upon the license that they should give a preference to the Canadian buyers, the resolution of the department was rescinded, and, to use the expression of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) the rescinding " synchronised " with the coming on of the provincial election. Owing to the agitation, I think, decision was suspended, and it never became operative afterwards. I am sorry my hon. friend who represents the county of Charlotte (Mr. Hartt) is not in his place, because I should like to give him an opportunity of explaining a letter which he wrote in this connection, which I propose reading. He wrote the Deputy Min-
TMr. Hazen.]
ister of Marine and Fisheries approving of this proposed policy, but suggesting that the change when made should be printed in the regulations ,so as not to attract the attention of the fishermen. My hon. friend did not remember any such letter, but afterwards he was good enough to send me a copy of it. I do not wish to do my hon. friend from Charlotte any injustice and I think it only right that the letter should be placed on Hansard so that the fishermen of Charlotte county may have an opportunity of judging as to the action of the hon. member in that respect, and the hon. member may also have an opportunity of explaining his action, if he desires so to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Did not the hon. member for Charlotte suggest that this be printed in the license so that the fishermen should know it?

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
If that were so, it would have been a most admirable desire on the part of the hon. member for Charlotte, but his suggestion was that it should be printed in the license so as not to attract the attention of the fishermen. It is a curious letter. Let me read it:
House of Commons, March 2nd, 1912.
A. Johnston, Esq.,
Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries,
Dear Sir,-Your letter of February 29th re the proposed change in the wording of "Weir Licenses'' received.
I approve of giving buyers for the Canadian sardine factories the second but similar privileges as the buyers of bait.
This will not injure the Canadian fishermen, but will make the supply to Canadian factories more certain. X think new licenses should be printed including this provision, and as licenses are not in the hands of fishermen yet, there must be time to make the change, and licenses that are in the hands of fishery inspectors X hope can be recalled and the new form sent out.
Please let me know if this can be done. I know the fishermen will pay less attention to the change if done in this way.
Yours truly,
T. A. Hartt.
What does that mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Does it mean that this
being printed in the license, and the fishermen seeing it there will recognize it as being correct, whereas, if it is not in the license, they will imagine something is being done which is improper and against their interests, and will suspect it is desired to keep them in the dark about it? That is what Mk. Hartt tells me he meant by it-that he wanted the greatest publicity given to it.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Yes, but the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hartt) has stated that it should ibe printed in the license, and he says:
I know the fishermen will pay less attention to the change, if done in this way.
If it is printed in the license they will pay less attention to the change.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is attaching to the word " attention " a different meaning from what the hon. member (Mr. Hartt) intended. What he meant to convey was that if this is printed in the license the fisherman will see it at once when he gets his license, he will know what the conditions are, and therefore it will give him less trouble, 'annoyance or worry than if this is not done laiter on when his attention is called to it in some other way. The word " attention " is being used in one sense by the hon. member for Charlotte and in another by my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley).

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: What other word would convey what was meant?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Perhaps he meant to say
" disturbed " or something of that sort. I think I would have phrased it differently.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Would be " disturbed " less?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Well I think that is
about what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hartt) meant. He meant that if it was printed in the license the fisherman would not realize that it had been done and there would be less dissatisfaction among them. It would not attract their attention. But the word " attention " is an ordinary English word the meaning of which is very well understood.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I think it is a most extraordinary thing to argue that the writer of the letter meant that it would not attract their attention so much if it was right there in the license where they could see it. Surely it was the very thing that would attract their attention.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
But if it were interlined the fishermen would see that the minister meant imposing upon them the obligation to give Sir William Van Horne's canning industry the first right to buy. In other -words, the policy which my right hon. friend determined upon at the request of Sir William Van Horne was that the fishermen would proceed with their catch first
to the American buyers and if the Americans offered $4 per hogshead, Sir William Van Horne's company would say that they would give $4 and then the fishermen would be obliged to sell to Sir William Van Home's company. In a few years the result would be that the American buyers would be driven out of the market completely and the fishermen would be at the mercy of Sir William Van Horne's company.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Would they be obliged to
sell?

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Yes, obliged to sell to the Van Horne Company at whatever price the American buyer would offer. Right up to time the fish are actually taken off, the Van Horne company had to have the first right, just as it was also provided with respect to bait. Such a condition was to remain in full force until the fish were taken from the weir and unloaded from the licensees' boats to the boats of the buyer., So that the fishermen were placed absolutely at the mercy of Sir William van Horne's company. The fishermen were greatly opposed to it. The hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Hartt) saw, as a sensible man, that it would be opposed by the fishermen. He was so anxious to encourage the establishment of Sir William van Horne's canning industry that he favoured the change, and he requested the deputy minister to see that the license was changed, and that the change should be actually printed in the license and not interlined as he believed it would attract less attention from the fishermen. He says:
I think new licenses should be printed including this provision, and as licenses are not in the hands of the fishermen yet, there must be time to make the change, and licenses that are in the hands of fishery inspectors, I hope, can be recalled and the new forms sent out. Please let me know if this can be done. I know the fishermen will pay less attention to the change, if done in this way.
I would say that what the hon. member for Charlotte had in mind was that if this restriction were interlined it would attract the attention of the fishermen and possibly cause an uproar among them, but if it were printed it would probably attract less attention.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
It is impossible for my hon. friend and myself to say what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hoitt) did mean. I am sorry he is not here, but from a conversation I had with him I think he meant the very reverse of the construction that my hon. friend places upon his letter. However, perhaps before the session is over, the hon.

member for Charlotte will have an opportunity of explaining. From what I know of the hon. gentleman, I know that he would not for one moment entertain the idea of doing anything which would not be in the greatest interest of the Ashmen and of the public generally.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: He is an old school teacher, and he knows what the word "attention" means.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Is that regulation still in force?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: No, it never wias in force.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Some months ago tenders were invited for a patrol service on the coast of Newfoundland. I am aware that a tender was put in by Captain Charles A. Stewart, of Wood's Island, Newfoundland. He received information from the depart ment that his tender was the lowest, but I was never table to ascertain whether a contract had been awarded. I had some correspondence with the deputy minister of the Naval Service on the subject, and the last I heard from Captain Stewart was that an inquiry wias being made at St. John's, Newfoundland, to ascertain whether his boat was suitable for the service.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: How long ago?

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: In April. Perhaps the minister would be good enough to write me a letter giving a statement with regard to the position of affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I will ask my officials to take note of it, and I will have the information sent to my hon. friend.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I know the department are very anxious to keep in Canada all the boats we have. Had they -anything to do with the sale of a steamer called the John Webster to the United States Government last month?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: That is a matter the Department of Naval Service has nothing to do with. It might come under the attention of the Marine -and Fisheries Department, but it has not come under my attention. I saw that a steamer named the John Webster bad been s-old to parties in the United States. The steamer was one that went between Brockville and an American port.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: A new steamer.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
If she -is a Canadian-registered steamer the registry could not be transferred to -the United States without the -approval of the department and the

apprpv-al would not be given without my sanction. It -has not come to -my -attention. Possibly the steamer was registered in the States, and that being so we should have nothing to -do with it. Does my ho-n. friend happen to know whether it was American or Canadian registry?

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
No.
M-r. HAZEN: If it is registered in the United States they -could sell it to whomever they choose without let or hindrance on our part. If it is registered in Canada, before Canadian registry can be clo-sed they have to get the consent of the department.
Fisheries Protection Service-To provide for new vessels, $100,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
I have kept that item in the estimates because it was in last year, but under existing conditions we do not intend to expend the money. We fee-1 we ought to have better Ashery protection o-n Lake Erie than we have -at the present time. We have o-n-e vessel, the Vigilant, but in spite of the greatest vigilance the Vigilant can exercise there is no doubt that there is more or less poaching from the American side.
This item was inserted to provide a faster boat for that service, but owing to the general cutting down of expenses we have not proceeded with that work, and we shall try to get along for another season.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Has the minister given up hope of having the treaty passed some years ago between the two nations, for the protection of these contiguous waters, ratiAed by the American Senate? It is a very valuable treaty and was pressed upon us by some Americans as vigorously as by our own people. I know that special interests have so far been able to prevent the ratiAcation of the treaty.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I think Canada went almost to the very limit it could go without humiliating itself with regard to the matter.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: And I might say to my hon. friend, in all candour, that I think there is practically no chance of it at all.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
At one time it looked as if Congress were about to consider the matter favourably, but, as the minister said, private interests intervened and were sufficiently inAuential in Congress to prevent ratiAcation. In reference to the Ashing in the St. Lawrence river, particularly in the

Thousand Islands where it is mostly sporting fishing, owing to the conflict of interests between the federal and provincial authorities, what was the business of both for a time became the practical business of neither, and Americans were fishing in our waters among the Thousand Islands with impunity. An arrangement was entered into, largely through the efforts of the Thousand Islands Anglers' Association, by which, while perhaps the letter of the law was not adhered to on either side, the fishermen on each side were controlled. It is difficult to say whether a fisherman is on one side of the line or the other, and thus many poachers escaped. Does the minister know anything about that arrangement and is it still being carried out?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: The Government of Ontario has taken over the administration of its own fisheries. Under the decision we make the regulations, but they are administered by the provincial government. We make the regulations at their request in matters of that sort.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: The province has nothing to do with the enforcement of the law on lake Erie.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Those are commercial fish. We prevent encroachment on our waters by people from the American side, but the province would have control so far as its own people are concerned.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I shall be glad when the Government can afford a swifter steamer on lake Erie because there is undoubtedly a good deal of poaching by fishermen from the other side.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Has the Government
changed its attitude in respect to extending the season for fishing every autumn? Regularly, particularly at election times, certain extensions in the open seasons are asked for. It is always suggested and argued that the season hau. been a bad one up-to-date, and that the fisherman will not have had the full fruition of his year's toil unless a certain extension is made.
vVhenever there has been a kind of undertone from the country that there is going to be an election, the fishing season has been bad, judging by the extensions. I think the minister made an announcement in the House at one time that they were not going to do that any more, that they were going to have a certain stated close season which was going to be adhered to, and that it would be fixed after all due
consideration. Would there be any chance this autumn of the minister extending the fishing season, or is he obdurate on that, and will he refuse to do anything?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: We will always be open to reason. If the hon. gentleman would advance good reasons, in the public interest, why it should be done, we will consider it. My hon. friend refers to what I stated in the House. I said I thought the close season should be fixed by statute. At present it is fixed by order in council. Practically every year there are demands for an extension of the fishing season.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Would it not be better to have it fixed by statute?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Perhaps it would be. I know the hon. members from Northumberland (Mr. Loggie), Gloucester (Mr. Tur-geon), and Kent (Mr. Robidoux) would not agree to that, because, they say, there are certain exceptional seasons when it would be a hardship to fishermen if an extension were not granted. A great many people are dependent on fishing for their livelihood, and when the seasons are not extended they are without the means of livelihood. subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Will the minister make a statement as to the regulations regard-

mg the size of lobster? Some years ago the late Colonel Tucker who represented St. John's county in Parliament, was appointed on a commission to examine into the whole question of lobster fisheries-I think that was the subject-and I remember how greatly he prided himself upon the fact that no lobsters could be caught of less length than nine inches. He took great credit for that. It occurred to me that his views were sound, because I understood that until a lobster reached that size it had not arrived at the age of maturity, and that it would prevent reproduction of a most valuable species, and would be very injurious to the public interest, if the small lobsters were killed. About two years ago I received a letter from a gentleman who carries on a large business in fish in St. John, enclosing me a little bit of a lobster about two and a half inches in length, which was a sample of lobsters of the waters of the province of Nova Scotia, which were on the market in St. John. It was a great surprise to me. I made inquiries, and I was informed that lobsters at that time could be caught of any size in the waters of Nova Scotia, whereas in the waters of St. John' and Charlotte they could not be caught of a less size than nine inches. The lobster fisheries are of enormous value. I think the	lobster is the	most	valuable
shell fish that can be found. It is in very great demand in all the cities of the United States, and before the war was in great demand in Europe. Canned lobster is a very great luxury, and is a most delicious article of food. I am sure the minister will agree with me that it would be a great pity to have any regulation which allowed the sale of these small fish, and I hope he will be good enough to make a short statement with regard to the regulations respecting the size of lobsters which may be caught.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is quite right. In St. John and Charlotte county there has been a limit for many years. There are no lobster factories in St. John and Charlotte-no licenses are granted lobster factories in either of those two counties.- The lobsters are accordingly shipped away, very largely to the Boston market for sale. The result of there being no lobster factories in St. John and Charlotte county is that in the last few years there has been a email increase in the catch of lobsters in those two counties. The lobsters which my hon. friend refers to in the store m St. John no doubt came from the

south shore of Nova Scotia, where there is no size limit to the lobsters that may be caught and canned. There are many canneries there, the business having been long established. It was claimed on behalf of the canners that fresh lobsters could not be sent to market and sold at a price which would he profitable to the fishermen. The season there is very much shorter than in St. uohn and other places where there is a size limit. I agree with my hon. friend as to the impropriety and undesirability of allowing the catching of immature lobsters, and I believe in a very short time it will be possible to pass a law that will prevent any lobster canneries existing in Nova Scotia at any point west of Halifax. When you get beyond that there is no line of railway across the country, and it is a very long distance for the oanner to bring lobsters around to Canso, and ship them to the United States. But we are right up to the time when it will be possible to prohibit the canning of lobsters altogether, and to enact a size limit such as we have in the counties of Charlotte and St. John.

I am told that they were caught in such large numbers that in some cases the factories could not handle them, and they were sent to other factories some distance further down the coast. This year the catch has been very small.

coast similar to those now in force in St. John and Charlotte counties.

The following is a statement with respect to this work:
Atlantic Coast, C.G.S. Acadia.-This survey is being conducted along the southeast coast of Nova Scotia, starting from Halifax harbour to modernize the present charts of that locality.
Lower St. Lawrence, C.G.S. Cartier.-The work of this party is being gradually extended eastwards from the river and work has now been completed as far east as Point des Monts on the north shore and Cape Chat on the south shore. It is intended to carry the work along the south shore embracing the route of vessels approaching the St. Lawrence, during the coming season.
Lake Superior, C.G.S. Bayfield.-During the coming,season it is intended to use this party in surveying the more exposed coasts of Lake Superior, in the vicinity of Caribou island and Michipicoten.
Lake Superior, C.G.S. La Canadienne.- This steamer, owing to her age and small power, is employed in surveying more sheltered waters. Last season she completed the survey of Nipigon bay. This year she will complete Black bay which was omitted in the general coast work. If time permits she will be moved to work in the North Channel of lake Huron.
Pacific Coast, C.G.S.	Lillooet.-This
steamer is working around Queen Charlotte islands and Hecate strait and it is proposed to continue in that locality.

speechtext: Every person is in favour of any reasonable vote for the Northwest Mounted Police. I was asking some questions as to the number and the Minister of Public Works gave me some explanation. I think it would be interesting if the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) would say a word about the Royal Northwest Mounted Police force. How many men have gone overseas and how many are in the force now?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
There was a very earnest desire on the -part of practically the whole force at the commencement of the war to enlist for service overseas. But it was not practicable for them all to do that because they were needed in the West. Especially during the past three years they have done very excellent work indeed. Occasionally, from time to time, we have permitted discharge a little in advance to men who wanted to enlist. How many men have enlisted and gone to the front? I am not prepared to say just how many. A few years ago we

increased the force by 500 or 600 men. The term of enlistment was altered at that time from three years to one year. I think nearly all of the men took their discharge at the end of the year. The force now is about 800. In view of the reduction in the military forces in Canada, authority has been given to increase the mounted police by about 500 men. In addition to that, f have had communication with the commit sioner as to the possibility of raising a regiment, or even a brigade, of cavalry, from the Northwest Mounted Police if the time should ever come when cavalry would be needied im any of the theatres of war. We have communicated with the War Office from time to time, but they cannot say at present that any mounted force is needed. However, the commissioner has been authorized to announce that it is the intention to permit enlistment of a mounted force should it eventually be necessary. Some preparation has been made with a view to carrying out this proposal, should it be practicable to do so. The force has been provided with machine guns and a certain number of motor care for expedition in case of certain contingencies that were at one time apprehended. I believe that at the present time the force is in a highly efficient condition. That is the report made to me by Commissioner Perry. I do not know of any further information that I can give, but if any hon. gentleman would like to ask any question, I shall of course answer it to the best of my ability.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I saw in a newspaper four or five months ago an article headed " The Passing of the Northwest Mounted Police It read as if the Northwest Mounted Police had been done away with. Am I mistaken in supposing that that is the case?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
They are not
done away with at all. Perhaps the article originated from the fact that the arrangements with the three Prairie Provinces, Alberta, Sackatehewan and Manitoba, were abrogated and the force is now used entirely for Dominion purposes. That was done upon the recommendation of the Commissioner who thought that in view of certain changes in the laws of the western provinces the men -were being called upon to perform duties which would not tend to keep the force up to that high degree of excellence which has always characterized it. Under a very old arrangement the force performed the duties of a local police force for the Northwest Territories and afterwards for the new provinces. Legislation in regard to the liquor traffic and other matters
was recently enacted and the Commissioner made reports to this effect: In the first place, that there was ample scope for the time and energies of the force in dealing with conditions as they presented themselves in time of war, and, secondly, that a force called upon to enforce local police regulations was hardly able to maintain the morale and the efficiency which had always been maintained in the past. He recommended that there should be consultation wiith the provincial government. Negotiations were carried on and an arrangement, by common consent of all the provinces, was made by which the amount payable by each province to the Federal Government for the services of the force was to be discontinued and on the other hand the force was to be entirely under the direction of the Commissioner and used for purely Dominion purposes. I imagine that this charge is the foundation of the report to which my hon. friend alluded.

join hands with my hon. friend and see if we cannot influence the obdurate hearts of Sir George Foster and Sir Joseph Pope. I have been for some time urging the case of a young lady, but I have been able to make no more impression than my hon. friend.

could not answer my hon. friend. I have not had much to do personally with these cases. subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I cannot give my hon. friend accurate information as to the number of the staff, but I know that it has been very considerably in creased, and contingent expenses in the way of telegrams and expenses of that character generally have naturally been very considerably increased since the war broke out. Sir George Perley has received, during all the time he has been over there, no salary whatever as High Commissioner, nor as Minister of - the Overseas Service, and I understand that he is not willing to receive a salary in either capacity, although there is a resolution on the Order Paper providing for a salary to him as Minister of the Overseas Service.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Does the right hon. gentleman not think it would be more becoming, and more seemly to Canada, for our High Commissioner to be Teally High Commissioner, and draw his salary, and not represent a constituency in Canada, when he is really not sitting in Parliament and not actually representing the constituency at all? He is acting in a treble capacity: He is member for Argenteuii; he is High Commissioner; and he is Overseas Minister of Militia. It seems to me it is placing too much of a burden on one man, particularly when he is not drawing any salary in any of these offices. It looks very much to me as though he should fill one capacity, and
the man who fills one capacity and does it well is doing about all that one man is able to do. It looks to me as though he were overburdened with duties. He cannot perform all these duties and do them properly. I submit, the High Commissioner should be the High Commissioner and should have a salary commensurate with the duties of the high position which he fills. He should not occupy the three positions I have named. I think that instead of considering a union Government the right hon. Prime Minister had better dis-unionize that position.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I think that particular union has worked very well indeed so far. With a good deal of what my hon. friend says, I should be inclined to agree. It must be remembered that Sir George Perley went over in June, 1914, intending to return in September of the same year. The war broke out, and he has remained at his post ever since, with the exception of a couple of months last year, when he visited Canada. The duties of the High Commissioner are very important, and sometimes pretty onerous. I know that he has had a great deal to do during the past three years by reason of matters connected with the war, and I agree entirely that his duties as overseas minister are also important and sufficiently onerous of themselves. I realize that the arrangement which has been going on for some months is not one that could be made permanent, but I hope my hon. friend will give us till after the session to consider what may be the future disposition, and to endeavour to effect some arrangement which will be satisfactory, even to his critical judgment.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
That is enlightening so far. It would appear that the Prime Minister has in his mind a change of some kind in connection with the High Commissioner-ship at London. I am not going to argue whether it ought or ought not to be made. To be frank, it has been rumoured that he was going to insist on the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) accepting that high position.
As the Prime Minister has intimated that something is going to be done in this respect after the close of the session, now would be a good time for him to take the committee into his confidence and tell us whether he is going to appoint the Minis- ' ter of Public Works as High Commissioner for Canada in London.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
I am afraid that my hon. friend's curiosity is quite too ex-

cessive. I really have nothing to take the committee into my confidence about just at present. I may say in reply to the member for Welland (Mr. German) that I see a good deal of force in his observation and that after the session is over 1 -will give my most careful 'and attentive consideration to what he has urged.
Miscellaneous-Amount required to meet expenses of the Technical Board appointed to consider questions relating: to the level of the Lake of the Woods, $8,000.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Has that work been finished?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
I think that the work has been finished; I am surprised that the amount is so reasonable. Hon. gentlemen will remember that the International Waterways Commission had referred to them a question with regard to the level of the lake of the Woods, affecting interests in Manitoba and Ontario and in the United States. It was necessary for that International Commission to arrive at what would ibe a proper minimum and a proper maximum level for the lake of the Woods, taking the season throughout. In order to decide this, they had to consider questions affecting navigation, power, fisheries. and many other matters. If the level of the lake were raised to a certain height, some land would be flooded, and there was a question as to what damages should be paid. Moreover, if the lake were raised to a certain level, certain advantages would result to people upon the United States side of the lake, while certain interests there would be injured; the question was how to adjust satisfactorily these various conditions resulting from the raising of the level. An immense amount of information was scattered among the departments in Ottawa-the Interior Department, the Department of Marine, the Public Works Department, and others-and in order to get that information consolidated and in such form as to be of use for the Canadian Commissioners, it was found necessary to appoint a Technical Board for that purpose. I was assigned by counc'l the duty of organizing the board and of acting as chairman. As a matter of fact, I was chairman only in the sense of organizing and consulting. The real chairman of the board, the one who had the scientific and technical knowledge enabling him to do the work far better than I could, was Mr. W. J. Stewart, Director of Hydrographic Survey. We had on that board also representatives of the Public Works Department -Mr. Cballies and Mr. Chapleau-together

with representatives of the other departments in which there was information of this kind. A great many meetings of this committee were held. It was found necessary to employ surveyors and others in order to get the necessary information together and be able to advise the Canadian members of the International Waterways Commission.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Outside of the surveyors, the personnel of the commission consisted of men who were at that time civil servants?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Yes; they got no extra pay for their .services. Certain clerical assistance, however, had to be provided; travelling expenses had to be paid, and certain surveyors and engineers had to be employed to take observations from time to time This item is for the purpose of covering that expense. I have been informed by members of the International Waterways Commission that the information thus obtained was invaluable-indeed, was indispensable; that without it, it would have been impossible to get along at all. The result has been that the International Waterways Commission has been able to come to an arrangement with regard to the many diversified interests that were affected-an arrangement that will work out satisfactorily and will be acceptable to the people of both countries.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: The result of the work of the commission was satisfactory to the United States Commissioners?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: The commissioners of both countries agreed to it, yes.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: And they have fixed the level?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Without land damages?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: They made some provision with regard to land damages, and with regard also to the water-powers on the lake and on the Winnipeg river, which is entirely, I think, in Manitoba. My understanding is that both the Canadian and the United States sections of the International Waterways Commission have been able to agree upon a finding that is mutually satisfactory.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: But this item does not include any provision for land damages?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: No. There may not be any land damages for a long time to come; indeed, there may never be any.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: The report has not yet been completed, but pending its completion the :hon. gentleman will remember that I read a summary of the results of the investigation not long ago. The report is being printed and will be distributed, but it is pretty voluminous and there will be some delay.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Has the Commission to which this item relates concluded its work?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
I do not think there will be anything more for the Commission to do. Its functions were to gather this information foT the use of the Canadian section of the Commission. That having been done, and an understanding having been arrived at, I do not think there will be anything further.

speechtext: I have had occasion to consult some of the geological survey reports of late, and I find that the translation is certainly of a high order. I understand that Mr. Sauvalle has been ill through the winter, and I trust that the department will take that into consideration and see that Mr. Sauvalle gets a good rest, because I am sure it would be difficult to find in the whole Dominion a man capable of replacing Mr. Sauvalle in the very important post of translator of such technical matter as the geological survey reports.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.

I can understand the item "collection of mining and metallurgical statistics,'' but I cannot understand what is being done under the heading of "Investigation of ore and other economic deposits, structural material, expenses of fuel and ore dressing plant," and I should like to see the expenditure under these three, heads,-separate, if possible. I know some-

thing about the mining busi-
9 p.m. ness, and I do not see what good is being done by this expenditure.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I thought it had reference to peat. We have been carrying on investigations along that line for a number of years, and, to my certain knowledge, nothing has come of it. As for the men that lay down our asphalt, they are perfectly capable of investigating for themselves. Nothing whatever has come of these investigations so far as I know.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Is the department still
making experiments with regard to peat?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I think they do work of this character. Where there is a well-founded rumour of the discovery of an important mineral, sometimes a rare mineral, like molybdenite, the Geological Survey makes, investigation and assists in procuring information which might be useful to show whether the deposit would be capable of commercial development. That is one thing which occurs to me at the moment. I am not sure about structural material. The collection of mining and metallurgical statistics is, of course, perfectly obvious.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
I quite understand the
last item, but where there is a discovery of any valuable ore the commercial interests of the country will very soon find out whether it could be worked on a paying basis or not. The mining men do not depend on any one else to tell them wheiner it is worth their while to work it or not. They see for themselves.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
I do not think my hon. friend has the right idea. I know something about this matter in my own province, and I can tell him that work of that character done by the Geological Survey has been worth a great deal to the people of the province. For example, in the determination of faults. In a particular district a fault will be in a particular direction and of a certain distance; in an adjoining district, under different geological conditions, the fault may be different-the push may be in a very different direction and of a different length. I am quite sure the Geological Sur-

vey of Canada in investigating that, which is only one, I dare say, of a score of features in which they have been of assistance, has rendered important service to those who come with a view to possible development. It is very important to a man who is operating a gold mine, for instance, if he strikes a fault, to know that the faults in that particular district mean a displacement for a certain, distance in a certain direction.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I quite understand that, but the mining men themselves employ geologists to find out the nature of the faults, and where to test for them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: In Nova Scotia it has been done to a very great extent by the Geological Survey, and the service which can be given by general survey of the whole province and an examination of the differences between, different districts is one that would hardly be rendered by private enterprise.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.

My right hon. friend
mentioned the possibility that some of this money was expended in connection with the development of properties /in which molybdenite, for instance, had been discovered.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.

In all these matters, where the mineral is of importance for war purposes, we act in thorough co-operation with the Imperial Munitions Board. I do not know what may have been done in the particular instance to which my hon. friend refers, but we have tried to act in absolute co-operation with the Imperial Munitions Board, in order that they may be supplied with all mineral necessary for their purposes.

speechtext: A careful study ought to be made of a region within close proximity to Ottawa known as the Gatineau region. Most members of this House are familiar with it. subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: What benefit does the country derive from the expenditure of $134,620 for the Mines branch and $430,020 for the geological survey? I think that the people would be very much interested in knowing what financial benefit the country derives from this expenditure. These services get information, it is true, but that information is of no financial benefit to the country. It may enable certain interests to go in and take possession of the land. The Government do not sell the land and they have no control over it. They may acquire some information which they give to private interests and by means of which the private interests derive some advantage, but how does any advantage come to the country? As stated by my hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), private interests find these things out themselves. I never could understand wherein the country was deriving any financial benefit commensurate with the very considerable expenditure that is being made from year to year on these surveys and explorations.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.

I believe that our debates are greatly lengthened by having desks in the chamber. In England no newspapers are allowed, and no writings except such as a member can take on his knee or on his hat, and the result is that the speeches are much more concise. If the desks were abolished you would have a more compact chamber, shorter debates, and speeches more to the point.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
I beg to differ with my hon. friend. Not that I care for desks, but I do not think they have the slightest influence in relation to the length of speeches. If you read the history of parliamentary eloquence in England you will find that at the beginning of last century, with Pitt amk Burke and Sheridan, the speeches were long and lasted sometimes for two of three days. If you read the debate on the famous case of Warren Hastings, not the trial but the debate, in which some of the finest addresses were delivered, you will see the debates were very long. According to Lord Curzon, who lectured on the subject of parliamentary eloquence at one of the English universities, it was only in the last
part of the nineteenth century that the speeches in the House of Commons became more matter-of-fact, and that the practice of making long speeches died out. To-day Asquith, Balfour, Lloyd George and all the leaders-there are no Sirs amongst' them, all the leaders of parliamentary eloquence-they are very short and pithy.

We acted entirely on the advice of Messrs. Pearson, Marchand and Ewart. They were all of one opinion, and the minister has to follow the united opinion of the architects in such a matter. It might be well to remember that the ministers of the Crown in the Old Land are represented in Parliament when details have to be explained, minor details particularly, by under secretaries, and the ministers can retire to their offices, go on with their work and attend 'to their correspondence. With us, if an item is being discussed in the House in which a minister or his department is at all interested, the minister must of necessity be in the House. I submit that both the members of the Government in Canada and the members of the House are in a somewhat different position from that occupied by a majority of the members in the British Parliament. The ministers of the Crown in Canada not only have their public duties jhere, but moist of them have a lot of correspondence outside of that as well. The unembers are in the same position. I suppose there is not a man in this House who Tias not a business he is trying to look after, iin a degree at least; and if he has a desk in the Chamber, a lot of his correspondence Is signed while he is sitting here, taking part-spasmodically it may be, but yet taking part-in the business of the House. If we were to have no desks in this House, the man who is actively engaged in business, as nearly every member of this House is, would have to absent himself from the House a good deal more than he does, looking after his correspondence. Speaking for myself, I think I do twenty-five per cent of my outside business while I am in the House. I think nothing of importance escapes me. But I would be in 
the House much less if I had no desk before me on which I could attend to these little matters when I have a moment or two in the House, t'o get them off my hands. These things will have to be considered. The position of members of Parliament in Canada, including the members of the Government, is not identical with the position of the majority of the members in the British Parliament.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
When the war broke out we in Nova Scotia were willing to give up all our public works. We had large votes in tile estimates, and even before the war began, on account of the fall in the revenue, we were advised that we should cease pressing for improvements that had been promised, or from pressing for the expenditure of money that had already been voted. We were told by the minister that large ex-
penditures had to be dropped; that practically all public expenditures that were not absolutely necessary were to cease. Accordingly, we have not been pressing the minister for any expenditure, although some of these works are very necessary. It has been brought to the notice of the House several times that the fisheries of Canada are becoming more important every day; that fish as a food commodity is of the highest importance. In order to catch fish, ample facilities must be provided in the way of harbours, wharves and breakwaters. Facilities of that kind are very much needed in the part of the country from which I come. There was a very substantial item in the estimates of 1910 and 1911 fo the opening of a harbour at Ashby Bay in the county of Victoria. The question of the opening of that harbour was before this House and the Government for a good many years, and at last they reached the conclusion that the harbour should be opened. It would not involve the expenditure of a great deal of money, and once it was opened it would be of the greatest importance to the fisheries and the trade of the country generally. The vote was dropped some years after this Government came into power. I did not press the matter very much then, by reason of the fact that the war had broken out, and there was a fall in revenue and great need for economy. But now, the Minister of Public Works is spending large amounts of money on St. John harbour, for instance, which is an old harbour which they have got along very well with for a great many years, and I venture to think they could get along fairly well with it- as it is now. Although a layman, so far as the engineering business is concerned, I wish to warn the minister that he may find he has made a very grave mistake if he expects to make a good harbour at St. John by building a breakwater across the harbour. We had a .trial of that sort of thing as a protection to the entrance through the Grand Narrows in the Bras d Or lakes. A breakwater was built with the expectation of diverting the current and getting calm water where a very rapid current used to run. A large amount of money was expended, hut the result was simply to make the thing worse than it was before. I -am simply warning the minister that by the building of this breakwater at St. John, the currents he disturbs may make the water more treacherous than before. I think the item providing for the expenditure of this large amount of money on an old harbour could very well stand over, and preference should -be given to

such places as I 'have mentioned, where there is crying need for improvements that could be made at comparatively small cost. If the minister would undertake this work, the fishermen, not only of my county hut of the whole coast of Nova Scotia and in parts of New Brunswick, where they go for mackerel, cod and other fish, would be given a shelter that would enable them to carry on their wo-rk very much more conveniently and at a greater profit than at present.
Now that the minister is starting out to spend money, I must, in justice to that part of the country -which I represent, emphasize as strongly as I can the necessity of restoring those votes in the estimates of 1910, 1911 and 1912, providing for substantial improvements of the character I have mentioned and going on with the work.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
If my hon. friend, who says that I am undertaking new work, will only look at the item he will see that there is a reduction in it of over $2,500,000, which is an evidence that we are adhering to our policy of economy during war time, even in such important matters as the great harbours of this country. The .harbours enumerated here are our national harbours. Before the outbreak of the war large contracts had been let for the purpose of improving the harbours to meet the trade requirements of the country, and the amounts here asked for are simply to carry out the contracts that were then entered into. I quite appreciate the importance of harbours such as my hon. friend has mentioned, and no one will be more pleased than I when conditions will allow me to restore .any vote that is required 10 p.m. in the interests of the fishing industry of Nova Scotia, or any other place. There was great need for additional accommodation at the harbour of St. John last winter. It is-our great winter port, and the traffic has greatly increased on account of the war. New docks are urgently required. Only a few months ago several ships had to lay off the harbour awaiting their turn to dock, so great was the need for additional dockage. We hope, with the money we are here asking for, to be able to complete the docks, now under way, in order to relieve the congested condition that has existed at the port of St. John for some time. In regard to the harbour of Victoria, the contract had been let and there was a pressing need for the completion of the work .at the earliest possible date. I can assure my hon. friend that when the opportunity presents itself t'he
needs of that part of the country from which he comes will not be overlooked.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
I might point out that the goods that were exported through St. John during the last winter season amounted in value to nearly $200,000,000. There has been an enormous development in the business of that port during the last two years. New wharves have been erected, but they are not yet capable of handling the tremendous business that is offering every winter. The expectation is that this winter the exports through {hat port will be even larger than last year, when they far exceeded the exports through the port of Boston. I want the committee to understand that the money that has been spent on these new wharves at St. John is not lost to the country. These wharves are revenue producers and when they have been completed, they are handed over to the administration of the Marine and Fisheries Department. Last year we collected at the port of St. John a revenue of something over $100,000 in round figures, and that figure will be largely increased during the present winter, and will go a long way, at 3J per cent, towards paying the. interest on the money that these wharves cost. It is absolutely necessary fox the protection of these wharves that the breakwater that was built many years ago and extends from Negro Point to Partridge island, should be extended the whole way across. Otherwise the wharves would be in danger of being destroyed. I would be the last to urge the Minister of Public Works to spend the public moneys at the present time unless It was for an absolutely necessary purpose, and this particular work, as I have pointed out, is absolutely necessary in order to protect the trade of the country and to protect the investment which the country now has in the wharves which have been erected there of late years, and which are substantial revenue producers for the public exchequer. Tenders for this work had been asked for before the war broke out-before there was any idea that war would be declared. ,
Tenders were received after the outbreak of the war, buit in view of the fact that it was felt that economy .should be exercised, the deposits made by the tenderers were returned to them, and it was decided not to proceed with the work. The action of the Public Works Department in proceeding with the work now is because of the fact that it is necessary in order to protect the country's property which was constructed at an expenditure of a good

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
I quite understand
that the hon. member from St. John, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, should stand up for his county and for his port. No one appreciates the enterprising people of St. John more than I do. At the same time, there is no use concealing the fact that the harbour of St. John is taxed beyond what God and nature ever intended it to be.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Not by any means.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Practically speaking,
it is not a harbour at all. It is just a sort of bay, into which the magnificent St. John river rushes, and where there is continually a battle royal between the tides of the Bay of Fundy and the rushing waters of the St. John river. That is the kind of harbour my hon. friend is trying to tame into a mill-dam for vessels to get into. We can have harbours anywhere where there is an island off the coast, if we get people generous enough to build any sort of structure between the mainland and the island, and then some extension beyond the island, but it is costing the Country too much, to satisfy the ambition of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. At the sartie time, I think it would be better to give more attention to places where there are harbours. I am sorry the magnificent harbour of Halifax seems to be forgotten to-night. There is also the magnificent harbour of Sydney and North Sydney, which nature intended as a harbour, hut it is neglected. No attempt is made to develop a number of places where there are proper harbours, but the minister asks to spend millions of dollars to fight the tides of the Bay of Fundy and the rushing torrents of the river St. John,

in order to make a harbour to please my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I am very much surprised that my hon. friend, usually a well-informed man, is so much at fault regarding the geography of the Maritime Provinces, and I extend to him an invitation to come to St. John this summer, when I am at home and may have the pleasure of entertaining him. I am sure when he looks over our harbour and its possibilities, that he will-I will not say apologize,-but he will admit he was wrongly informed and making a mistake in crying down one of the great harbours of Canada. I think it is a great pity that a Nova Scotian should cry down the harbour of St. John, and I think it is a great pity that a New Brunswicker should decry the harbour of Halifax, I do not think that is the way to promote the interests of the Maritime Provinces. I think we should give credit to one another, and help one another, having more of a feeling of patriotism for our own province ratner than seek to spread disunion and create discord in reflecting upon the merits of the different localities. My hon. friend is a bit of a joker, I know, and says things in a facetious way; but it is really absurd to speak as the hon. gentleman has spoken of the port which *has been selected as the terminus of the Canadian Pacific railway on the Atlantic coast and from which goods to the enormous value of nearly $200,000,000 were shipped last -winter. The fact I have just mentioned carries with it the refutation of what my hon. friend has said in regard to the merits of the port. I think the port of St. John has enormous possibilities, not only because of its geographical position, but because of the enterprise of the people and because of the fact that the Canadian Pacific railway, the greatest of Canadian carrying companies, has made it its terminus on the' Atlantic coast, which will lead to its constant development year by year, and to an enormous increase in the traffic which will pass through it. So far as results are concerned, St. John is to-day, without question, the greatest port on the Atlantic coast.

speechtext:
We have been asking the farmers all through the West and all through Canada to produce more in order that the Allies may be fed. One of the greatest requisites to production on the farm or anywhere is the expedition and cheapness with which those products can be shipped to the market. I notice there is nothing in these items for elevator accom-

modation at Quebec, Saint John, and Halifax.

speechtext:
I	remember the
railway estimates. An elevator system should be a part of the development of those harbours. The elevator system which is being constructed by the Railway Deparxment is part of the Government railway system, as the Halifax elevator is part of the Government railway system- We are not making a concentrated effort in the development of our harbours to make them in uniformity and have them completed harbours when we are through. At the head of the Great Lakes there are a large number of elevators- On this side of the Lakes there are a large number of elevators. We have spent millions of dollars in Canada to get through lines of transportation by land. Without elevator accommodation at Quebec, Saint John, and Halifax, a portion of the year when those railway facilities could be used -and navigation its closed is of no avail to- us at all. At the present time, there is no means of rushing by rail the products of the West and having them stored at Quebec, say, during the winter, awaiting navigation-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
There is a million-bushel
elevator at Quebec now.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
But that is a smallsized elevator for the purpose required. It is only the size of the elevator at the head of the Welland canal.
Mr- COCHRANE: That is a two-million-bushel elevator.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
It started out as one of 500,000 bushels. The foundations were provided so that enlargement could be made, which has since been done. With a two-million-bushel elevator at the head of the Welland canal, a one-inillion-bushel elevator at Quebec is of minor importance. In order to encourage the farmer in the West to produce we have to complete our transportation facilities to the seaboard, otherwise there is no use building railways to the seaboard, and there is no use urging the farmer to produce because he cannot get his product to the seaboard. Then you will tell me that there is no tonnage to take it '.across when we get it there. I think the honourable member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), a year ago, brought up the matter, which I consider of
very great importance. At that time, if the Government had taken some means of providing against what was inevitable, the loss of tonnage, and had gone on with the erection of elevators, we should have been in a magnificent position to encourage the farmers of the West to produce, because we not only could have taken their grain to the seaboard but we would have had elevators to handle it and a certain number of ships to carry it across. My honourable friend the Minister of the Naval Service (Mr. Hazen) informed us to-day that the shipyards of Canada were largely engaged in building ships of various capacities for the Imperial Government. It is our duty to do that but we ought not to leave the other undone. I believe, as much as I believe anything, that the whole country would have been well served, and perhaps better served, if we had set the shipbuilding capacity of Canada to work constructing ships a year or two ago for Canada herself, either through private or Government enterprise; because at that time when the submarine menace was becoming very serious we might have looked sufficiently far ahead to realize that one of the difficulties of our Allies would be to get their food supply, through lack of tonnage. Even at this moment, because we do not know when the war is going to cease, it would not be out of place for the Dominion Government to utilize certain of the shipbuild- -ing establishments for the construction of vessels for ourselves to carry the products of the country overseas. The United States is doing a good deal in this way but she is not doing it for us; she is doing is for herself and the Allies. The links in our transportation system are altogether lacking when we have not elevator facilities at the seaboard and when we do not seem to be making any provision to secure tonnage to carry our products overseas.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
In so far as giving consideration to the carriage of the products of the farmers is concerned, I think the Government can reasonably claim that they have taken a very great interest in matters of that kind. With respect to the question of elevators, we have built for the producers of western Canada large interior elevators which are of great benefit. We have also established a Government terminal elevator at Fort William and we have established practical control of all the elevators at that terminal, which control is sufficient to regulate all the conditions incident to the transport of our grain through the elevators at that point. My hon. friend quite

appreciates, I am sure, that so far as the producer of western Canada is concerned, he is almost entirely dependent upon the elevatovr space at Fort William and Port Arthur. The space at the points named is quite sufficient at present to take care of the trade of western Canada. I quite appreciate the importance of additional elevator space at the seaboard, at such points as St. -John and Halifax, but I do not see that any special purpose can be served by additional elevator space at Quebec, for example. Quebec is only a summer port, and any grain stored in an elevator at Quebec in the fall, or at the close of navigation, would have to remain there until navigation opened in the spring. It would be of very little importance in the matter of the placing of grain whether it was at Quebec or at Port Arthur or Fort William. By placing it at Quebec you would probably have the long rail haul which would make it very expensive to the producer, and I do not think it would be a point at which additional elevator space would be particularly necessary. There is no doubt that we should have additional elevator space at St. John but the Canadian Pacific have already a large elevator there and the Government have erected one in connection with the Intercolonial railway. If my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) is assured that there is a pressing need for elevator space at a point of that kind, I am sure he will meet the requirements as soon as it. is possible for him to do so.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
For many years the Canadian people have been spending millions of dollars deepening harbours and building docks at different ports, not only on the Great Lakes but on the seaboard, and whenever a harbour has been completed or a splendid dock erected, with possibly great elevators for the storage of grain and sheds for facilitating the handling of the products of the farms, we discover that some privately-owned railway controls the right of way along the docks and this railway, in its selfishness, places all sorts of obstructions against other railways. It would be well that every precaution should be taken to see to it that the nation shall own the right of way and the railway tracks to all harbours in Canada and provide for running arrangements so that privately owned railways shall be able to receive and discharge freight on these docks without being hampered by another privately owned road which would naturally look after its own business. Is the minister making provision for this in the new works that are going on

at these harbours not only on the Great Lakes but on the sea coast?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I do not know to what points my hon. friend makes particular reference when he says that privately owned railway companies are in possession of the right of way and. obstruct others from getting access to the harbour, where1 the work has been constructed by the Government. Now that we have a Railway Commission, it has full power and authority to deal with and regulate any conditions such as my hon. friend suggests. If there is any particular point at which the difficulty that he mentions exists, I am sure it will only be necessary to bring it to the attention of the Railway Commission. If the Railway Commission has not sufficient power to regulate such a condition, if the complaint is genuine, as I am sure it is or my hon. friend would not have mentioned it, then I can assure him that the Government will be only too glad to take it up and find a remedy in some form or other.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I have no special reference to any particular port or railway. 1 think it is generally admitted that this has been the policy for years, and everybody in the trade knows that a railway is always able to hamper other railways, notwithstanding the efforts of the Railway Commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Of course they will do that if they can.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Have the works at River St. Charles been resumed?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Owing to the policy of economizing as much as possible, a portion of the work under the existing contract is being delayed, but a portion has been resumed; that is the providing of a bridge across the river, which was necessary, and preparation for the erection of a shipbuilding plant under the programme of the Imperial Munitions Board, which awarded contracts for the erection of four ships to parties at Quebec. The board have been in communication with the Department of Public Works for some time with a view to getting a piece of ground which we had expropriated there, for the purpose of establishing a shipbuilding plant.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Representations have
been made to the minister in connection with a public building fur a post office and custom house at Thorold, and I was given to understand there was to be something in the estimates for that purpose. Thorold

is a growing town, with large numbers of extensive factories, and the post office facilities are absolutely inadequate for the public service. It is almost imperative that there should be a public building there for post office and customs purposes. I trust the minister will have something in the supplementary estimates for this and will at least make a beginning this year, even if he does not have money enough to complete the enterprise.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I should be very glad to accommodate my hon. friend but, in view of the existing conditions, I am afraid it will he impossible, especially as I have not one single new item in the estimates.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: What about the Cardinal building?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: That is the only one, and it was arranged for previous to the change of policy of the Government. When we come to the next item I hope my hon. friend will give me credit for practising economy in the construction of public buildings. I hope the day is not far distant when we shall be able to accommodate my hon. friend at Thorold.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: In the Island of Cape Breton, there are quite a number of telegraph lines owned by the Government, and they are very useful institutions, serving an excellent purpose in many sections where there are no other telegraph lines. I understood it was the intention of the department to change these telegraph offices into telephone offices. Is that so? And have any been converted?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
It was the desire to make many changes along that line, but they have not been made up to date because we have been keeping down expenses and putting off the work from time to time.
In the Supplementary estimates we are making some extensions in Cape Breton, and I shall be very glad, when the deputy is here, to give any information that is available in the department in reference to the telegraph system of the Maritime Provinces.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
In the county of Inverness there is practically a new line running from Margaree through lake Ainslie into Whyeocomagh and on, connecting with the Intercolonial at Orangedale. It is quite a lengthy line and very serviceable indeed. This place called Lake Ainslie is my birthplace, and I am quite familiar with the conditions there. There is a settlement
about ten miles along the east side of this beautiful lake, and I think they have only one office in the ten miles. There has been a good deal of negotiation back and forth in the effort to get another office. There is a place of resort and a fishing place called Trout Brook, where there is a little hotel, and where many people go, and a telegraph office near that point would be a great convenience and would be of great public service. The minister might inquire as to some of his friends who might get the office there; I am not seeking for patronage, but only want to see that this public convenience is put in the most central place in that part of the county, particularly on account of the great number o.f strangers who go there and sometimes desire to communicate with the outside world. The nearest telegraph office would be at Whyeocomagh or the first telegraph office on the other side of this place at three miles down. It is not a matter of very great expense, and I wish the minister would make a note of it and see that something is done.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
I think I had this matter before me two or three days ago, and on the recommendation of the officers of the department some action was taken-just exactly what it was I have no idea-with a view of meeting the necessity which appears to exist, which my hon. friend describes. I shall be glad to take a note of it, and get the details.
In reference to item 142, "Public Works- Miscellaneous-$936,641.50," hon. gentlemen will find a reduction of eleven or twelve millions, so they will see how full of economy we are, in reducing the expenditure during war time. This item was passed -the other day.
Life saving stations, including rewards for saving life, $125,400.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: How many of these on the Pacific, and how many on the Atlantic?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: In British Columbia, four; Ontario, ten; New Brunswick, four; Nova Scotia, fifteen; Quebec, one, and Prince Edward Island, five.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Might I renew my humble request that life-saving stations be established around Gaspe?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: ACTIVITIES OF THE NAVAL SERVICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
I will be glad to make a note of the suggestion.
